title: She Heard Heaven First
paragraphs:
She Heard Heaven First
Why Rebekah Heard God Before Isaac Did—and What It Reveals About the Quiet Ways God Still Speaks Today
There are moments in Scripture that make us uncomfortable—not because they are unclear, but because they overturn the assumptions we carry about how God is "supposed" to work.
This is one of those moments.
A man who walked in the footsteps of Abraham.
Yet when the future of God's covenant family stood at a crossroads...
That single detail has been quietly sitting in Genesis for thousands of years, waiting for readers to slow down enough to notice it.
Perhaps you have missed it before.
But once you see it, you will never read the story the same way again.
Because this is not merely the story of a family conflict.
It is the story of divine sovereignty overcoming human preference.
It is the story of grace interrupting tradition.
It is the story of heaven rewriting expectations.
Before the Twins Were Born, Heaven Already Had a Plan
Genesis tells us something heartbreaking before it tells us something miraculous.
Isaac and Rebekah could not have children.
Twenty years of wondering whether the covenant would continue.
"Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife because she was barren."
But the pregnancy was unlike anything she expected.
The children struggled violently within her.

The Hebrew text uses the verb רָצַץ (rāṣaṣ), carrying the idea of crushing, bruising, or violently pressing against one another. This was not ordinary movement. The conflict was so severe that Rebekah cried out in confusion.
"If this is so, why is this happening to me?"
She does not complain to Isaac.
She does not seek human advice.
"She went to inquire of the LORD."

וַתֵּלֶךְ לִדְרֹשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה
Vattelekh lidrosh et-YHWH.
The verb דָּרַשׁ (darash) means far more than asking a casual question.
Genesis 25:23 records one of the most astonishing prophecies in Scripture.

"Two nations are in your womb,
and two peoples from within you shall be divided;
the one shall be stronger than the other,
and the older shall serve the younger."
This completely reversed the customs of the ancient Near East.
But God had already announced His decision before either child had done anything good or evil.
The apostle Paul later explains why.
"Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue..."
God's purposes are never controlled by human customs.
Isaac Never Forgot Esau's Hunting Skills
Genesis quietly inserts one revealing sentence.
"Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game."
But Scripture had already revealed something earlier.
God Himself had declared His choice.
The tragedy is not that Rebekah favored Jacob.
The tragedy is that Isaac appears willing to bless Esau despite the revelation God had already given before the twins were born.
Genesis 27 paints an aging Isaac preparing to pass the covenant blessing to Esau.
Yet nowhere in the chapter does Isaac seek the Lord again.
Meanwhile Rebekah remembers what God had spoken decades earlier.
Hearing God Is Not the Same as Holding Authority
This story has often been misused to argue about power.
Scripture is not teaching that women are spiritually superior.
Nor is it teaching that husbands are unnecessary.
Rather, it demonstrates something seen throughout the Bible.
God is completely free to speak through whomever He chooses.
The issue has never been status.
The issue has always been surrender.
Rebekah's actions in Genesis 27 remain deeply troubling.
No careful reading of Scripture should celebrate deception.
The Bible records these actions honestly without calling them righteous.
In fact, the consequences are devastating.
Rebekah never appears to see him again.
Sin always leaves scars—even when God ultimately fulfills His purposes.
This is one of the great distinctions of Scripture.
The Bible reports human failures truthfully without endorsing them.
God's sovereign plan advances not because deception is good, but because His purposes cannot be defeated by human weakness.
That is the scandal of grace.
God's Choice Was Never About Human Worthiness
Paul returns to this account in Romans.
Yet God's covenant continued because salvation has never rested upon flawless people.
It has always rested upon a faithful God.
This reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The Greek word for grace is:
It is God's freely given favor toward those who cannot earn it.
Everything in Genesis whispers toward Calvary.
There, the true Firstborn voluntarily took the place of undeserving younger brothers and sisters.
There, Jesus accomplished what no patriarch ever could.
There, grace rewrote humanity's story forever.
Why This Story Still Matters Today
Have we stopped seeking Him the way Rebekah did?
She did not receive revelation because she possessed greater authority.
She received revelation because she went to inquire of the Lord.
God has never stopped speaking through His Word.
The Holy Spirit continues to illuminate Scripture for those who humbly seek Him.
The question is not whether God still leads His people.
The question is whether we still seek Him above our preferences.
The other remembered what God had already spoken.
How often do we resemble Isaac?
How often does comfort drown conviction?
How often do our traditions become louder than God's Word?
This family was anything but perfect.
If this story were written by human imagination, it would probably end in tragedy.
But Scripture tells a different story.
Because Scripture ultimately points beyond Isaac.
The One who entered humanity's broken family tree.
The One who carried every scandal to the cross.
The One who conquered sin, death, and shame.
The One who still rewrites broken lives today.
That is why our theme is not merely a slogan.
It is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Perhaps your family story feels fractured.
Perhaps you carry regrets that seem impossible to undo.
Perhaps you've made choices you wish you could erase.
Genesis reminds us that God does not excuse sin—but neither is He defeated by it.
The cross stands as the greatest proof that God's redemptive purposes are stronger than humanity's failures.
If this article stirred your heart, don't let it end here.
Sometimes the article you share becomes the answer to someone else's prayer.
Your support enables us to continue creating deeply researched, Christ-centered articles, biblical studies, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered content that reaches hearts around the world.
Tell us what stood out most, or simply write, "Lord, help me hear Your voice." Your testimony may strengthen someone else who reads it.
Return to it when you need to remember that the Lord still speaks through His Word, still keeps His promises, and still accomplishes His purposes even through imperfect people.
Because long before we learned to search for God, He was already writing a better ending.
